problem_statement:
Regression in 4.5.0: nested recursive `discriminatedUnion` throws `Maximum call stack size exceeded`

### Summary

A `discriminatedUnion` that reaches itself through a getter throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` in 4.5.x — but only when the union is **nested inside another schema**. As the root schema it parses fine, and in 4.4.3 it parses fine either way.

This is the same shape as #4444 (closed) and produces the same `escapeRegex` → `$ZodLiteral.init` frame as #4994 (closed), so it looks like a regression of a bug that was fixed once.

### Reproduction

zod only, no other dependencies:

```js
import * as z from "zod";

const Geometry = () =>
  z.discriminatedUnion("type", [
    z.object({ type: z.literal("Point"), coordinates: z.array(z.number()) }),
    z.looseObject({
      type: z.literal("GeometryCollection"),
      get geometries() {
        return z.array(Geometry());
      },
    }),
  ]);

const point = { type: "Point", coordinates: [1, 2] };

Geometry().safeParse(point); // ok

z.object({ geometry: Geometry() }).safeParse({ geometry: point }); // RangeError
```

| zod | as the root | nested in an object |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4.4.3 | ok (1 ms) | ok (1 ms) |
| 4.5.0 | ok (2 ms) | **RangeError** |
| 4.5.4 | ok (1 ms) | **RangeError** |

Any nesting triggers it — `z.object`, `z.looseObject`, `z.array`, `.optional()`, `.nullable()`. A plain `z.union([z.string(), Geometry()])` does not.

### Stack

```
RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
    at String.replace (<anonymous>)
    at Module.escapeRegex (zod/v4/core/util.js:260:16)
    at zod/v4/core/schemas.js:1890:55
    at Array.map (<anonymous>)
    at zod/v4/core/schemas.js:1890:14
    at $ZodLiteral.init (zod/v4/core/core.js:65:9)
```

### Impact

[`zod-geojson`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/zod-geojson) composes `GeoJSONFeatureSchema` and `GeoJSONFeatureCollectionSchema` exactly this way, so on 4.5.x both spend about eight seconds and then throw — on an empty feature collection, before any real data is involved:

```js
import { GeoJSONFeatureCollectionSchema } from "zod-geojson";

GeoJSONFeatureCollectionSchema.safeParse({ type: "FeatureCollection", features: [] });
// ~8 s, then RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
```

Its simple schemas (`GeoJSONPointSchema`, `GeoJSONLineStringSchema`, `GeoJSONGeometrySchema`) are unaffected and parse in ~2 ms. Both zod-geojson 1.7.0 and 1.7.1 behave identically, so the version of that package is not the variable.

For a browser app this is worse than a thrown error: the eight seconds are spent on the main thread, so the UI freezes before the parse fails.

### Environment

- zod 4.5.0, 4.5.1, 4.5.2, 4.5.4 — all bad; 4.4.3 good (first bad release: 4.5.0)
- Node v24.14.0, Linux

problem_statement:
Excessive memory retention in v4 memoizer

We are seeing a severe memory regression after upgrading Zod from 4.4.3 to 4.5.4 in a large Backstage monorepo.

The workload is a repository-wide ESLint run:

```sh
yarn eslint . --no-cache
```

With Zod 4.4.3 it completes normally:

```text
Elapsed time: 49.16s
Maximum RSS: 5,487,520 KB
Exit status: 0
```

With Zod 4.5.4, even with an 8 GiB limit, it eventually runs out of memory:

```text
Elapsed time before OOM: 181.32s
Maximum RSS before OOM: 8,723,528 KB
Exit status: 1
```

The final GC cycles look like this:

```text
Mark-Compact 8042.9 (8224.5) -> 8027.5 (8225.2) MB
Mark-Compact 8043.5 (8225.2) -> 8028.1 (8225.7) MB

FATAL ERROR: Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit
Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory
```

I traced the regression to the `lastCtx` / `lastBucket` cache in `src/v4/core/memoizer.ts`.

Current code:

```ts
let lastCtx: object | undefined;
let lastBucket: Map<object, Entry> | undefined;

// ...

let bucket: Map<object, Entry>;

if (lastCtx === ctx) {
  bucket = lastBucket!;
} else {
  bucket = bucketFor(state, inst);
  lastCtx = ctx;
  lastBucket = bucket;
}
```

Removing this additional cache and always retrieving the bucket from the parse state fixes the problem:

```ts
const bucket = bucketFor(state, inst);
```

With that change applied to Zod 4.5.4:

```text
Elapsed time: 48.44s
Maximum RSS: 5,621,244 KB
Exit status: 0
```

Here are teh results:

| Version | Result | Time | Maximum RSS |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| 4.4.3 | success | 49.16s | 5,487,520 KB |
| 4.5.4 | OOM | 181.32s | 8,723,528 KB |
| 4.5.4 with cache removed | success | 48.44s | 5,621,244 KB |

The comment above the cache says that the bucket is memoized "for one parse", but `lastCtx` and `lastBucket` are captured by the closure created in `attach(inst)`. This means the most recent context and bucket can remain reachable for the lifetime of the schema instance.

The per-parse state already keeps the bucket, so the extra `lastCtx` / `lastBucket` fast path appears to extend the lifetime of parse-local data unnecessarily.

Is there a reason this cache needs to live on the schema instance rather than relying on `bucketFor(state, inst)`?

problem_statement:
Accept enum-typed targets in z.toZod

Fixes #6524.

`z.toZod<T>()` rejected `z.enum(SomeEnum)` against a property typed `SomeEnum`, with the unhelpful diagnostic `expected: SomeEnum, received: SomeEnum`. TypeScript doesn't consider an enum reference identical to the union of exactly its own members, and the union is the only output type `z.enum` can infer from `typeof SomeEnum` — so no schema could ever satisfy an enum-typed property. The equivalent member-union target worked, which is the asymmetry the issue reports. This was also flagged during review on #5913 and hit by a user in the first canary.

The fix keeps exact identity as the fast path and adds a fallback: rebuild the `string | number` part of each side through a mapped key type (`{ [K in T]: K }[T]`), which collapses the enum-reference/member-union difference and nothing else, then re-check identity. The walk recurses only through types identical to their own homomorphic rebuild, so every guarantee the exactness decision in #5913 protects is preserved — `any` (explicit guards), `readonly` and optional modifiers, intersection-vs-flat, brands, member subsets, and plain `"A" | "B"` literals against a nominal enum all still fail. Enum targets now work at any depth, including arrays, tuples, records, nullables, and recursive types.

Type-only change: zero runtime, memory, and bundle delta. The fallback only instantiates where the fast path already failed, so typecheck cost lands on error paths and newly-valid enum paths; the repo's own typecheck time is unchanged.

problem_statement:
z.emoji() accepts strings that contain no emoji

### Problem

`z.emoji()` accepts strings that contain no emoji at all:

```ts
z.emoji().parse("123");        // passes
z.emoji().parse("#");          // passes
z.emoji().parse("*");          // passes
z.emoji().parse("\u{200D}");   // lone ZWJ, passes
z.emoji().parse("\u{FE0F}");   // lone variation selector, passes
z.emoji().parse("\u{1F3FD}");  // lone skin tone modifier, passes
```

The pattern is `^[\p{Extended_Pictographic}\p{Emoji_Component}]+$`. `\p{Emoji_Component}` is not a set of emoji — it is the set of pieces that combine with one: ASCII digits `0`–`9`, `#`, `*`, regional indicators, skin tone modifiers, ZWJ and variation selectors. A string built only from components is not an emoji.

problem_statement:
Wrong translation for French.

Hi!

When we use the format `iiii do MMMM yyyy`, we should have this translation:

"Jeudi 1er août 2019" and "Jeudi 29 août 2019"
but we have:
"Jeudi 1er août 2019" and "Jeudi 29[**ème**](#) août 2019"
                                                           
There is an extra "ième" when the day is greater than 1, this should not happen.

[src/locale/fr/_lib/formatters/index.js](https://github.com/date-fns/date-fns/blob/master/src/locale/fr/_lib/formatters/index.js) is not included / loaded and use the wrong format (`Do` instead of `do`). I didn't know how to do it. `formatters` is not used when I place it in the `locale`... and the engine seems to ignore it...

It does not break the functionalities but it's a bad "experience" for users... I can replace it if French, but... 😄 

Regards

**EDIT**:
New link in v3: https://github.com/date-fns/date-fns/blob/main/src/_lib/format/formatters/index.ts#L317

problem_statement:
roundToNearestMinutes roundingMethod producing unexpected results

When using `roundToNearestMinutes` function the rounding method doesn't seem to produce an expected result, or maybe there is something I'm missing.

For Example
`const result = roundToNearestMinutes(new Date(2022, 6, 24, 0, 28, 59), {
  nearestTo: 1,
  roundingMethod: "floor"
});
console.log(result);`

Produces
Sun Jul 24 2022 00:29:00 GMT+0800 (Singapore Standard Time)
Expected
Sun Jul 24 2022 00:28:00 GMT+0800 (Singapore Standard Time)

`const result = roundToNearestMinutes(new Date(2022, 6, 24, 0, 28, 59), {
  nearestTo: 1,
  roundingMethod: "ceil"
});
console.log(result);`

Produces
Sun Jul 24 2022 00:30:00 GMT+0800 (Singapore Standard Time)
Expected
Sun Jul 24 2022 00:29:00 GMT+0800 (Singapore Standard Time)

problem_statement:
assertIsRequestId is a no-op for all non-number invalid types (only throws for NaN)

### Description
The JSON-RPC request-id validator in the WebSocket message parser is meant to reject anything that isn't `number | string | null`, but its boolean logic only ever throws for `NaN`. Booleans, objects, arrays, and `undefined` all pass as valid request ids and flow downstream into `clientSubscriptions` Map keys and error messages.

### Root cause
`packages/server/src/unstable-core-do-not-import/rpc/parseTRPCMessage.ts`:
```js
if (obj !== null && typeof obj === 'number' && isNaN(obj) && typeof obj !== 'string') {
  throw new Error('Invalid request id');
}
```
`typeof obj === 'number'` combined with `typeof obj !== 'string'` (always true once the former holds) plus `isNaN(obj)` means the throw fires only for `NaN`. Git history shows the original (PR #508) was correct -- `if (typeof obj !== 'number' || isNaN(obj))` -- and the boolean got inverted when the type was widened to `number | string | null`.

### Steps to reproduce
```
NaN          -> throws (correct)
true         -> passes (should throw)
{}           -> passes (should throw)
[]           -> passes (should throw)
undefined    -> passes (should throw)
```

problem_statement:
httpLink / httpBatchLink don't create their own AbortController, so unsubscribe doesn't cancel the request (same pattern as #7389)

#7390 (closing #7389) fixed `httpBatchStreamLink`: it created its own `AbortController` and passed it into `jsonlStreamConsumer`, but the observable's cleanup was a `// noop`, so `abortController.abort()` never ran on unsubscribe and the JSONL stream kept consuming from the server after the subscriber disconnected.

I checked the other HTTP links and this same shape exists in two more:

- `httpLink.ts`: passes `signal: op.signal` straight into `universalRequester`, no internal controller, cleanup is `// noop`.
- `httpBatchLink.ts`: passes `allAbortSignals(...batchOps.map(op => op.signal))`, still only combining caller-provided per-op signals, no internal controller, cleanup is also `// noop`.

Compare with the links that already do this correctly: `httpSubscriptionLink.ts` and `localLink.ts` both do `raceAbortSignals(op.signal, ac.signal)` with their own `ac = new AbortController()`, and call `ac.abort()` in their cleanup. `httpBatchStreamLink.ts` now does the same after #7390.

So `httpLink` and `httpBatchLink` are the two remaining HTTP links that rely entirely on the caller supplying an `op.signal` that happens to fire on unsubscribe, instead of owning their own controller tied to the observable's lifecycle the way every other link in the package does. Whenever the caller's `op.signal` isn't already wired to this specific subscription's teardown, the underlying fetch outlives the subscriber — same wasted-bandwidth/dangling-request consequence as #7389, just without a streamed body to make it as visible in the network tab.

problem_statement:
WebSocket link silently ignores the operation AbortSignal (removeEventListener with no matching addEventListener)

### Description
An `AbortSignal` passed to a WebSocket operation (`op.signal`, exposed via the `signal` request option) is never wired to anything. Aborting the caller's signal does not cancel an in-flight request nor stop a subscription. This diverges from `httpSubscriptionLink`, which honors `op.signal`.

### Root cause
`packages/client/src/links/wsLink/wsClient/wsClient.ts`: the `request()` teardown calls `signal?.removeEventListener('abort', abort)`, but there is no matching `signal.addEventListener('abort', ...)` anywhere in the `wsLink` client directory (`signal` appears only at the destructure, the type, and the `removeEventListener`; no `signal.aborted`/`throwIfAborted` either). The `removeEventListener` removes a listener that was never added. The v11 refactor (PR #6223) plumbed `signal` into `request()` but only added the cleanup half.

### Steps to reproduce
Subscribe over a WS link with an `AbortController`, then `ac.abort()`. Observed: no `subscription.stop` frame is sent and the subscription keeps running; an in-flight WS query/mutation is likewise not cancelled. Expected: abort tears the operation down (and sends `subscription.stop` for subscriptions).

problem_statement:
bug: `httpBatchStreamLink` AbortController is created but never called on unsubscribe

### Provide environment information

**Package:** `@trpc/client`
**File:** `packages/client/src/links/httpBatchStreamLink.ts` (lines 75, 139, 216)
**Version:** v11.17.0

### Describe the bug

In `httpBatchStreamLink`, an `AbortController` is created and passed to `jsonlStreamConsumer` to signal cancellation of the JSONL response stream. However, the observable's cleanup function is a noop:

```ts
return () => {
  // noop
};
```

`abortController.abort()` is never called when the observable is unsubscribed. As a result, the underlying response body stream continues consuming data from the server after the subscriber has disconnected — wasting bandwidth and holding the stream open unnecessarily. It can also cause `observer already completed` errors if the stream later resolves after the observer has been cleaned up.

### Link to reproduction

https://stackblitz.com/github/trpc/trpc/tree/main/examples/next-minimal-starter

### To reproduce

1. Set up a tRPC app using `httpBatchStreamLink`
2. Initiate a query that takes >1s to stream (e.g. a procedure returning an async iterable)
3. Unmount the component or navigate away before the stream completes
4. Open DevTools → Network tab
5. Observe the request continues streaming to completion despite the subscriber being gone

### Additional information

Root cause: In `packages/client/src/links/httpBatchStreamLink.ts`, an `AbortController` 
is created and passed to `jsonlStreamConsumer`, but the observable's cleanup function 
is a noop — `abortController.abort()` is never called on unsubscribe.

Suggested fix (one line):
// Before
return () => { // noop };

// After  
return () => { abortController.abort(); };

The AbortController is already wired into jsonlStreamConsumer — only the cleanup 
call is missing. Fix applies to all three batch paths in the file (~lines 75, 139, 216).

problem_statement:
Standardize separator and casing used in locale names

The separator we use for locale names seems to be inconsistent. Some locales like Swahili use the underscore for their locale names: https://github.com/arrow-py/arrow/blob/d515e7463700b7da4c89caf81bcb736395abf898/arrow/locales.py#L4308-L4314. Others like Croatian use the hyphen: https://github.com/arrow-py/arrow/blob/d515e7463700b7da4c89caf81bcb736395abf898/arrow/locales.py#L4393-L4395.

As for casing, Hebrew seems to capitalize `IL`, but others do all lowercase: https://github.com/arrow-py/arrow/blob/d515e7463700b7da4c89caf81bcb736395abf898/arrow/locales.py#L3225-L3227.

These should be standardized and validated in a test case.

problem_statement:
Add week_start parameter to floor() and ceil()

<!--
Thanks for taking the time to submit this feature request.

Please provide us with a detailed description of the potential improvement.
-->

## Feature Request

I would like to be able to specify the day of the week in the `floor` and `ceil` functions, e.g.

```
firstday = month.floor('week',week_start=7)
```

For now I am doing this as a workaround:

```
firstday,_ = month.span('week',week_start=7)
```

which is essentially all that `floor` is doing anyway, so it looks like it should be possible to just pass along a `**kwargs` in both `floor` and `ceil` so that they also get all of the other optional functionality of `span`.

problem_statement:
exponential wait issue

The exponential waits functions with a max value perform exponential backup followed by constant polling, exactly as designed.  In my use case, I need exponential backoff up to 60 seconds followed by polling every 60 seconds forever.

The exponential wait functions compute 2^attempt_number, then return the max value (60) when 2^attempt_number exceeds 60.  However, after a few days, 2^attempt_number gets very very large. 

Revise the exponential wait functions to simply return max if the last returned value was max, skipping the unnecessary computation.

problem_statement:
Coalesce multiple ORs into a single object

In our codebase, we have cases of many conditions for retrying. Tenacity has been a massive improvement over what we used before.

For example:

```python
        (
            retry_if_exception_type(httpx.ConnectError)
            & retry_if_not_exception_message(message="[Errno -2] Name or service not known")
            & retry_if_not_exception_message(
                message="[Errno -5] No address associated with hostname"
            )
        )
        | (
            retry_if_not_exception_type(httpx.ConnectError)
            & retry_if_exception_type(_EXCEPTIONS_TO_RETRY)
        )
        | retry_if_result(_should_retry_request)
```

Since we have so many conditions, we occasionally need to debug this logic, and the many OR are implemented as two argument calls, resulting in a chunk of calls in the call stack which all look the same. It is painful.

OR is implemented by `retry_any`, which is computed in the following way:

```python
    def __call__(self, retry_state: "RetryCallState") -> bool:
        return any(r(retry_state) for r in self.retries)
```

This is great, as it supports an OR of many conditions.
Unfortunately, it combines like this (from `retry_base`):

```python
    def __or__(self, other: "retry_base") -> "retry_any":
        return other.__ror__(self)

    def __ror__(self, other: "retry_base") -> "retry_any":
        return retry_any(other, self)
```

This results in `self.retries` only having two items.

If `__or__` were specialized in `retry_any`, it could "flatten" the call stack by passing all current items in `self.retries` to the new `retry_any`.

This also applies to `retry_all`.

AFAICS, this should have no performance cost.

X ``` Currently produces: ```html

``` Both paragraphs should appear before the table, in input order, but the second ends up inside the row. These cases also affect table sections and fragment parsing. Also foster parenting needs to respect an intervening template instead of moving content outside the older table. And: column-group fragments can incorrectly close their parsing context. Setting either of these as a `colgroup` element’s HTML should produce just `

`, without introducing row or column-group wrappers: ```html ``` Also an errant `` incorrectly closes the current column group, splitting subsequent columns into another group. EOF handling in column-group mode also needs to follow the normal body/template cleanup rules. The root cause is that fragment parsing currently uses a copy of the context element as its stack root. That can introduce redundant structure. For example, setting a `tr` element’s HTML to `` nests another row instead of producing just ``. It can also leave parsed nodes outside the result container during streaming, only moving them back at fragment completion.

Name normalization can trim control characters and apply Unicode case folding

Currently some parser paths use `Normalizer.normalize(...)` for names that require narrower rules.

The current implementation trims with `String.trim()` and lowercases with Unicode rules. That can remove control characters from accepted tag and attribute names, and can make non-ASCII names compare as equal to ASCII names. The HTML5 spec has tag and attribute names as ASCII case insensitive.

For example, these should not equal:

```text
"data-x\u0001"
"data-x"

"K"
"k"

"ſ"
"s"
```

HTML name comparisons should use ASCII-only case folding. XML parsing should preserve exact names unless the configured parse settings request ASCII folding.

This affects tag and attribute identity, duplicate detection, selector matching, and contextual parser choices.

ParserConfiguration should support max number length

The default max length will be 1000, configurable via API to a positive int value, or disabled (any number size allowed).

Number length checks will be added to the BigDecimal and BigInteger access methods, where appropriate.

Potentially unsafe deserialization in JSONObject#fromJson() static fields are not excluded

This behavior may be security-relevant when `JSONObject#fromJson(Class<T>)` is used on untrusted input, so I am reporting it here as a public issue in line with the repository's published vulnerability-reporting guidance.

In release `20251224`, `JSONObject#fromJson(Class<T>)` iterates `clazz.getDeclaredFields()`, calls `Field#setAccessible(true)`, and assigns matching JSON values without excluding `static` fields:

https://github.com/stleary/JSON-java/blob/cf653682be81e5ff630c8ac5527a5060b9a813e8/src/main/java/org/json/JSONObject.java#L3365-L3378

As a result, deserialization can write not only per-instance state but also mutable declared class-level state on the caller-selected target type, subject to normal runtime access restrictions. That expands the binding surface beyond ordinary object population and may have integrity implications in applications that use `fromJson()` with untrusted JSON.

If helpful, I can provide a minimal reproducer and a regression test. A straightforward mitigation appears to be skipping static fields during binding.

Number parsing - de-duplication of logic

Logic to parse number is duplicated in XML and JSON parser.
They can be moved to single place and be referred by both.
